questions.q: Name the technological innovation that made it possible to transport perishable food (like meat and butter) across oceans in the late 19th century.
questions.a: Refrigerated ships (or "reefers") — first successfully used for meat from America and Australia to Europe in the 1870s–1880s. A wrong answer like "steamships" shows the student confuses general steam-powered transport with the specific breakthrough that enabled perishable cargo; "railways" indicates they miss the oceanic dimension.

questions.q: Why did British colonial policy in India shift from importing manufactured goods to exporting raw cotton and wheat in the mid-19th century, and how did this affect Indian peasants?
questions.a: The American Civil War (1861–65) cut off British cotton supplies, so India was forced to expand raw cotton exports; later, the Suez Canal (1869) and railway network made wheat exports profitable. Peasants were compelled to grow cash crops, reducing food grain acreage, increasing vulnerability to famine (e.g., 1876–78). A wrong answer that cites "industrial revolution in India" reveals confusion — India was deindustrialised, not industrialised, under colonial rule.

questions.q: A plantation owner in Trinidad in 1850 needs labour after slavery abolition. He recruits workers from India under a five-year contract. What is this system called, and what were TWO key features that distinguished it from slavery?
questions.a: System: Indentured labour. Features: (1) Contractual — workers signed a fixed-term agreement (usually 5 years) with specified wages, unlike chattel slavery; (2) Legal right to return passage after contract (though often denied in practice). A wrong answer like "it was voluntary migration" misses the coercion (debt, deception, penal sanctions for breach) and the racialised regulation that made it a "new system of slavery."

questions.q: Compare the causes of Irish migration (1845–1855) and Indian indentured migration (1830s–1917). Identify ONE structural similarity and ONE key difference in the role of the state.
questions.a: Similarity: Both driven by colonial/imperial economic policies that prioritised export/commercial interests over local food security (Irish grain exported during famine; Indian land revenue demands forced cash-crop cultivation). Difference: Irish migration was largely a desperate, unregulated flight with minimal state assistance; Indian indenture was a state-organised, regulated system (British colonial government licensed recruiters, set terms, provided ships) to supply labour to other colonies. A wrong answer that says "both were voluntary" ignores the coercion in both — Irish by starvation, Indians by debt and recruiter deception.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Nineteenth-century globalisation benefited all regions equally by lowering food prices and increasing availability." Use evidence from at least two regions to support your judgment.
questions.a: The statement is false. Evidence: (1) Europe/USA benefited — cheap grain and meat imports lowered living costs for industrial workers. (2) India suffered — forced export of wheat/cotton during famines (1876–78, 1896–97) raised domestic prices, causing millions of deaths; deindustrialisation destroyed artisan livelihoods. (3) West Africa: shift to cash crops (palm oil, cocoa) made economies dependent on volatile world markets. A wrong answer that cites only European gains shows inability to assess uneven impacts — a key board exam skill.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (1800–1914) with FIVE dated events that show the deepening integration of global food and labour markets. For each event, write one sentence explaining its significance.
questions.a: Expected timeline (sample): 1815 — End of Napoleonic Wars opens era of free trade; 1834 — British Slavery Abolition Act triggers indentured labour system; 1845–52 — Irish Potato Famine causes mass migration to USA; 1869 — Suez Canal opens, cutting Europe-Asia shipping time; 1870s — Refrigerated ships enable global meat trade; 1914 — WWI halts first globalisation wave. Significance sentences must link each event to food/labour flows. A poor answer lists battles or political events without economic significance, showing the student cannot identify the drivers of globalisation.
